attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, about the stocks in his June 24 tweet.

semantics.note: Faithful to the source. The proposition keeps the scope ('those stocks'), the 'most' quantifier, the June 25 date and the Micron exception. 'Again' points back to the June 24 decline.

contract.note: The contract reads the claim plainly and fairly: the fixed chart set, more than half down against the June 24 close, and Micron up. The real problem is missing data (the basket and the time of observation), not how the words are read.

evidence.note: A June 25 report from the day itself. It confirms Micron rose about 15% on earnings and that Nvidia, Broadcom, Apple and the Nasdaq fell. It cannot show that most of Marcus's unknown basket was down.

reviews.rationale: The Micron exception is backed by same-day reporting, and the wider tech weakness fits the claim. But the chart's stocks were never recovered, and there are no matched June 24 and June 25 prices for the whole set. So whether 'most' were down cannot be checked.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement in his post, made with 'no doubt in my mind'.

semantics.note: The claim is firm: many AI things are overvalued. The deflation clause only qualifies it and predicts no timetable. The proposition captures both parts and adds nothing.

contract.note: Marcus names no population and no valuation method, so the result depends on what the evaluator chooses for both. The contract's demand for comparison against fundamentals is a fair reading of 'overvalued', and it rightly refuses to stand in a single stock basket or a single price multiple.

evidence.note: Bank of England report from July 2026, before the cutoff. It says valuations look stretched on some measures but also cites strong earnings. That is not a fundamental-value finding for Marcus's unspecified group on June 25.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence is official commentary that some valuations look stretched, hedged with positive earnings news. No matched comparison of market prices against fundamental values exists for a defined AI population on June 25, so the evidence neither confirms nor refutes widespread overvaluation.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words introducing his chart in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful to the source. It keeps 'most', 'significantly' and 'for the month' as written, without inventing a rolling window.

contract.note: Treating 'for the month' as June to date and 'significantly' as a substantial loss is an ordinary reading. The contract admits the result could depend on which time window is used and on the missing stock list. Borderline cases are left unresolved, which is fair.

evidence.note: MarketWatch report from June 25, after the close. It shows Microsoft down about 21.6% for June so far, and all seven 'Magnificent Seven' stocks down for the month. These figures come from after the post went up, and the stocks in Marcus's chart are unknown, so this is context only.

reviews.rationale: Broad June weakness in big tech fits the claim. But the chart's stocks and time interval were never recovered, and month-to-date returns for the actual set are not established. Whether most were down significantly cannot be determined.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Under the policy, 'I don't expect' is a flat expectation, so this is a scored forecast that LLMs won't disappear anytime soon. The drafter's 'unlikely' modality wrongly makes it look hedged; 'will_not' fits better. The hedged 'may eventually be seen as ludicrous' clause is rightly left out.

contract.note: The plain reading (LLMs stay available and in use, and retiring individual models doesn't count) is fair. There is no deadline, and only a cessation across the whole industry would settle the claim early.

evidence.note: Vercel's own report, published October 15, showing heavy production LLM traffic through September. It fits with LLMs persisting but cannot close a forecast that has no deadline.

reviews.rationale: 'Anytime soon' sets no deadline, and the only early resolution would be a documented end to LLM use, which has not happened. LLMs remained in heavy use through September 2026, which is consistent with the forecast. A forecast with no deadline cannot be marked supported at an interim date.
